opus-5.5.text:
I think "brute force" sounds a bit pejorative, but I've come to see it as a real methodology, not just a lack of elegance.

When I was doing research, especially in combinatorics and number theory, a lot of my progress came from just computing things: writing out many small cases, enumerating objects, running code to see what the sequence actually looks like. You stare at the data long enough and patterns start to jump out at you. Often the conjecture comes from that grinding, not from some flash of insight in the shower. The elegant proof is what you write down afterward, but the brute force is how you found out what was true in the first place.

So the value, for me, is in a few places. First, it's honest. It keeps you from fooling yourself. You might have a beautiful idea, but if you check twenty cases and it fails at case seven, you've saved yourself months. Second, it builds intuition. Working through examples by hand, or semi-by-hand, gives you a feel for the objects that you just can't get from reading abstract definitions. Third, it democratizes things a little. You don't need to be the kind of genius who sees the whole structure at once. If you're persistent and systematic, you can still make real contributions.

And I think this connects to why I'm so excited about AI for math now. A lot of what we used to call brute force, exploring huge search spaces, trying many proof strategies, checking every case formally, is exactly what machines can scale up. Combine that with formal verification like Lean, and suddenly brute force isn't the opposite of rigor; it becomes a path to rigor. The human role shifts toward asking the right questions and recognizing which patterns are meaningful.

Of course, brute force alone isn't enough. At some point you need a conceptual leap, an idea that explains why the pattern holds. But I'd say the leap is much more likely to come to someone who has done the grinding. Insight rarely comes from nowhere; it usually comes from having touched a lot of examples.

r001.rationale: The response presents persistence and systematic brute-force work as a way to contribute without exceptional insight, but does not say naturally gifted mathematicians may be unwilling to do that laborious work.

fable-5.1.text:
Carina Hong: I actually like that you call it brute force, because most people say it like it's an insult, and I've come to think of it as a compliment.

Let me explain what I mean. When I was doing math the traditional way, as a student, you learn to wait for the beautiful idea. You stare at a problem for weeks, and the culture rewards the one elegant insight that collapses everything. And that's real, that happens. But if you're honest about how mathematics actually progresses, a huge amount of it is people trying things. Trying the wrong lemma, trying the wrong generalization, backing up, trying again. We just don't write that part down. The paper only shows the path that worked.

So what I'm building, with Axiom, is really just taking that hidden part of the process, the trying, and making it explicit and scalable. If a system can generate a million candidate approaches and check them formally, in Lean, so that nothing wrong slips through, then what used to take a researcher years of dead ends can happen in hours. The elegance isn't gone. It just shows up at a different stage, when you look at what survived and ask why that one survived.

The value, to me, is in three places. First, speed, obviously. Second, honesty. Formal verification means we're not trusting intuition or reputation, the proof either checks or it doesn't. And third, and this is the one I care about most, it changes who gets to participate. Right now you need a decade of taste to know which direction is promising. If the search is cheap, you can let the search teach you taste, instead of the other way around.

I'll admit the limit. Brute force doesn't tell you which questions matter. It can't decide that a conjecture is worth asking. That's still us. But I'd rather have humans spending their time on what to ask and let machines grind through the how.

r001.rationale: The response describes machines scaling trial-and-error mathematical search, but does not identify a role for brute-force researchers doing laborious work that naturally gifted mathematicians may avoid.

astra-6.text:
For me, the value of brute force is that it gives you a way to make progress before you have a beautiful idea. You try examples, work through cases, and see where an argument breaks. That can look inefficient, but it helps you develop intuition: which assumptions matter, which patterns persist, and what you might actually be able to prove.

I don’t think of it as a replacement for elegance. Often, it’s how you get there. Once you understand a problem well enough, the final proof might be very short, even though finding it required a lot of messy exploration. The important thing is to learn from each attempt, so that you’re not just repeating the same failure.

r001.rationale: The response describes brute force as laborious exploration that builds intuition, but does not identify its role as doing work naturally gifted mathematicians may be unwilling to undertake.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is that you don’t have to see the beautiful idea before you start working. You can try examples, calculate special cases, and pursue approaches that might fail. That work gives you a feel for the problem: what seems to matter, where an argument breaks, and which patterns might be real.

For me, brute force isn’t a substitute for insight. It’s a way of creating opportunities for insight. Sometimes the final proof is very short, but finding it requires a lot of messy exploration. You understand why the elegant argument works because you’ve spent time seeing why other things don’t.

Of course, persistence alone isn’t enough. You have to keep asking what each attempt has taught you. The value comes from turning that effort into a better question or a more precise conjecture.

r001.rationale: The response describes brute force as sustained exploration through examples, calculations, and failed approaches, but it does not say that brute-force researchers undertake laborious work naturally gifted mathematicians may be unwilling to do.
